title: InterQ-RL: Interaction-Aware Correction of Execution Mismatch in Quantized Agentic RL
trick: After matching the trainer's quantizer to the engine's, weight each action token's loss by the clipped product of engine-versus-trainer log-prob ratios over all earlier actions, dialed down where those ratios concentrate on few tokens.
framing_stripped: Called 'interaction-aware correction of execution mismatch in quantized agentic RL'; it is (a) quantization-aware training of the GRPO learner so that its forward reproduces the vLLM FP8 W8A8 and per-token-per-head FP8 KV cache-write rule bitwise, and (b) a detached importance weight on each action token equal to the exponentiated, $\sqrt{n}$-clipped sum of engine-minus-trainer log-probabilities over every earlier policy token in the same episode (observation tokens skipped), then shrunk toward 1 per action segment in proportion to a normalized effective-sample-size score under a fixed total squared-displacement budget (sec. 3.1-3.4, Algorithm 1).
load_bearing_assumption: That the engine and the learner condition on the same token history $h_t$, so that every rollout-learner discrepancy is a numerical path difference between two forwards of the same checkpoint ('two evaluations of the same checkpoint along different numerical paths', sec. 3.2) and the engine's returned $\log r_{\mathrm{exec}}(x_t \mid h_t)$ is the behavior policy's log-probability of the text the trainer sees; and that after QAT the residual $\delta_t$ is small enough (median K3 0.029 vs BF16 0.0014, sec. 3.1) that a log-envelope of $\pm 0.05 \sqrt{n_t}$ is a correction rather than a truncation. If the engine's conditioning state is not the text (eviction, compaction, cache edits), eq. 3 no longer factors over the realized prefix and the weight corrects the wrong quantity.
weakest_component: The headline 'matches BF16 within 0.7 points' and the +6.0 over QAT on ALFWorld are a single-seed, final-six-checkpoint difference that exists because the QAT arm regresses late (95.5% at step 300 to 89.6% at step 400 while InterQ-RL stays at 95.5%, sec. 4.2, Fig. 5); the paper's own Appendix D says independent-seed replications cover only BF16, QAT and InterQ-RL on ALFWorld and WebShop and reports no numbers from them. Second, three of four baselines are hostile reimplementations: 'No public implementation of AIS or QuRL was available during our experiments; we therefore reimplemented both methods from their papers' and 'Because QuRL does not specify the truncation cap $C$, we use $C=2$ in all QuRL runs' (App. C.3), so QuRL's collapse at step 278 is a collapse of the authors' QuRL. Third, the allocation rule (the part that separates InterQ-RL from the collapsing 'Prefix' and 'Global' variants, 37.3% and 22.4% at step 400 vs 95.5%, App. C.4) is motivated by one hand-picked segment pair ('We selected the pair by searching for a near-tie in $C_s$', App. B.2) and ablated on one environment with one 4B model. Fourth, the paper's own ruler cannot grade its result: 'A low K3 alone does not imply strong task performance' (sec. 4.2). Fifth, whether endpoint evaluation runs the policy in BF16 or W8A8-KV8 is not stated ('all evaluation decodes greedily', App. C.1), so the headline may compare a quantized-trained policy served at full precision.
regime: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on ALFWorld (3,553 training games, 134 valid_unseen for curves and endpoints, 30-turn cap, 24,576-token context, 20,480-token response budget) and WebShop (11,587 training instructions, 500 official test, 15-turn cap); Qwen3-8B (thinking disabled) and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (MoE) on ScienceWorld (1,819 official test variations, 100-turn cap, 40,960 / 50,176-token context, 32-token action cap). GRPO, 400 optimizer steps, batch 16 prompts x 8 responses, lr $10^{-6}$, PPO clip 0.2, dual-clip 10, KL coefficient 0.001, temperature 1.0 rollouts, greedy evaluation; verl + vLLM, FSDP (4B) or Megatron-LM (8B, 30B), 8 H20 GPUs per dense run and 16 for 30B-A3B. Rollout quantization: blockwise FP8 E4M3 W8A8 ($128 \times 128$ weight blocks, $1 \times 128$ activation blocks; lm_head, embedding and MoE gate excluded) plus per-token-per-head FP8 KV cache. Pass-rate band: ALFWorld success 64.1-97.1 (BF16 97.1, InterQ-RL 96.4, QAT 90.4), WebShop success 44.4-54.0, ScienceWorld solved 63.9-76.9 (Table 1). Episodes stop at the response budget ('when appending the next observation would exceed this budget, the episode stops at the response boundary', App. C.1): no eviction or compaction ever occurs. Mismatch scale: median K3 1.03 (unaligned W8A8-KV8) to 0.029 (QAT) to 0.0014 (BF16) over the final 20 steps (sec. 3.1); allocated $\alpha_s$ spans 0.372-0.989 over a run (App. B.4).
information_asymmetry: (1) Same text, different engine state: here $q_{\mathrm{old}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{exec}}$ are both evaluated on the realized token history $h_t$, so $\delta_t$ measures a numerical path difference and the prefix sum $E_t$ is an exact-identity correction (eq. 3-4). Under KV-cache eviction the engine's conditioning state at step $t$ is not any token sequence: attention entries for evicted tool outputs were computed while they were visible and are gone, while the trainer recomputing from text (full transcript or transcript-with-deletions) sees a state the engine never had. The engine still returns $\log r_{\mathrm{exec}}(x_t \mid \text{its own state})$ at sampling time, so $\delta_t$ remains computable from existing logs, but it now carries a conditioning-set term of unknown size on top of the numerical one; this paper measures only the numerical one (K3 0.029 after alignment) and its clip envelope $\pm 0.05 \sqrt{n_t}$ is sized for it. The open quantity, the size of $\delta_t$ by turn offset since the last eviction against the numerical floor, is CL-W43-11's probe C-W43-25, and InterQ-RL's prefix-sum machinery is a ready-made instrument for it. (2) What the trainer cannot see: the operation sequence (which entries were evicted, when) exists only in the engine; the trainer's input is 'all turns of an episode ... as one concatenated sequence' (App. C.1). InterQ-RL needs nothing from the engine beyond per-token log-probabilities, which is exactly why it cannot distinguish numerical mismatch from conditioning mismatch; a trainer that also received the operation log could reproduce the engine state (one prefill per trajectory under segment-batch attention, per card 2610.28577) and make the history factor exact again. (3) Per-token vs per-turn: Fig. 4 colors 18,683 action segments by interaction turn and shows current-action and prefix ratios separating with depth, but the paper reports no ratio-by-turn curve; under eviction the natural axis is offset since the last drop, and that curve is absent from the literature. (4) Training vs evaluation precision: K3 is measured on engine samples during training; whether the endpoint policy is served quantized is unstated, so the 0.7-point gap is between training recipes, not between served policies. (5) Within-paper regime gap: by design no episode ever exceeds the context window (it stops at the response boundary), so the paper's rollouts are precisely the no-eviction regime; the claim's regime (compaction or eviction inside the rollout) is one its machinery can be pointed at but was never run in.
occupies: Published and no longer claimable: the formal split of the rollout-learner trajectory ratio into a history factor and a current-token factor for multi-turn agents (eq. 3-4), the observation that alignment of the learner's quantizer to the engine's leaves a residual mismatch (K3 0.029 vs 0.0014) that compounds over the policy history, a bounded prefix-product importance weight over policy tokens with an ESS-based per-action allocation that fixes a displacement budget, and its evaluation against token-local corrections (Flash-RL TIS, AIS, QuRL) on ALFWorld, WebShop and ScienceWorld with 4B-30B Qwen3 under FP8 W8A8-KV8. For CL-W43-11 this occupies the 'trainer-side correction at the history level' half: the second, history-dependent off-policy term the claim's if_true predicts is already written down and corrected for the case where engine and trainer see the same tokens and differ only numerically. It does not occupy the conditioning-set case (eviction, compaction, cache edits), the ghost-information comparison (KV drop vs the same drop as text, C-W43-24), the measurement of divergence by offset since a drop (C-W43-25), or the operation-log-as-trajectory-record consequence.

neighbors.title: FP8-RL: A Practical and Stable Low-Precision Stack for LLM Reinforcement Learning
neighbors.trick: Run the rollout engine in blockwise FP8 W8A8 with an FP8 KV cache recalibrated every step, and patch the resulting rollout-trainer gap with a token-level truncated importance weight; the W8A8-KV8 stack this card's paper adopts, with the current-token-only correction it argues is insufficient for agents.

neighbors.title: AIS: Adaptive Importance Sampling for Quantized RL
neighbors.trick: Treat the FP8 rollout mismatch as exploration early and bias late, and mix the uncorrected and importance-weighted gradients per batch by a coefficient built from ESS, divergence and variance diagnostics; single-turn math and planning, token-level ratio, the direct baseline (92.3 vs 96.4 on ALFWorld) and the source of the ESS idea.

neighbors.trick: Put the trainer's forward in the same FP8 flow as the rollout so the two forwards agree and no inter-step calibration or correction is needed; the alignment-only line this card's paper runs as its QAT arm and shows regresses late in multi-turn agents.

neighbors.title: Rethinking Importance Sampling in LLM Policy Optimization: A Cumulative Token Perspective
neighbors.trick: Correct each token's gradient with the product of per-token ratios up to that position, clipped in log space with a bound growing as $\sqrt{t}$, as the unbiased lower-variance alternative to the full-sequence ratio; the envelope InterQ-RL borrows, applied to policy-version drift in single-turn tool-integrated reasoning, not to engine mismatch or observation-interleaved histories.

neighbors.title: Diagnosing Training Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning via a Zero-Mismatch Reference
neighbors.trick: Build a rollout path that reproduces the trainer's token probabilities exactly and use it as the zero-mismatch control to show that small numerical disagreements alone collapse training; the control arm that would separate numerical from conditioning-set mismatch, which neither this paper nor CL-W43-11 has run.

theme_fit.why: rollout-engine quantization (FP8 weights, activations and KV cache in vLLM under verl) as the cost lever for long-horizon agent RL, and the rollout-learner mismatch it creates inside the training stack, with a per-token ruler (K3) and a correction that needs no extra forward

a history-level importance correction for multi-turn GRPO and the late-regression dynamics of alignment-only training; supplies the incumbent and the exact-identity vocabulary (history factor vs current-token factor) for CL-W43-11's second term
same words (context, history) but the policy's context is never edited; observations are masked from the loss, not compacted

limitations_as_complaints: Every number for Flash-RL, AIS and QuRL, and every ScienceWorld number, comes from one seed: 'Independent-seed replications of BF16, QAT, and InterQ-RL on ALFWorld and WebShop yield conclusions consistent with the reported comparisons. Compute constraints limited broader multi-seed coverage across the remaining arms and ScienceWorld settings' (App. D), and no replication numbers are shown.

The baselines I beat are my own reimplementations with a guessed hyperparameter: 'No public implementation of AIS or QuRL was available during our experiments; we therefore reimplemented both methods from their papers' and 'Because QuRL does not specify the truncation cap $C$, we use $C=2$ in all QuRL runs' (App. C.3); the QuRL collapse at step 278 is on that code.

The mismatch ruler I report does not track the thing I care about: 'A low K3 alone does not imply strong task performance: QuRL's K3 falls as it collapses, while Flash-RL and AIS end with K3 values of 0.0071 and 0.0107 despite lower success' (sec. 4.2), so there is no scalar that says when history-level correction is needed.
